name: Recalls and Post-Market Performance
blurb: How AI devices perform after clearance.
title: Recalls and Post-Market Performance
answer: Evidence before clearance is often thin, few AI devices were supported by randomized trials, and post-market monitoring is where problems surface. Studies of FDA cleared AI devices find recalls in roughly 6 percent, mostly for software problems, which is why regulators want real world performance monitoring, especially for models that keep learning.

reading.body:
About 6.3 percent of FDA cleared AI devices have been recalled, mostly for algorithm or software problems, which shows that clearance is not proof of performance.

The pattern is that pre-market evidence for AI devices is often thin, and few were supported by randomized trials. Problems surface after deployment, not before. That is the argument for real world performance monitoring, and it matters most for models that keep learning, because a cleared model is not a fixed object.

The practical consequence for a medtech team is to monitor performance by site and population after launch. Drift tends to appear first where the data differ most from training. The WHO has described how makers and regulators should collect and act on this kind of post-market data.

The data covers one recall rate, one study, and one guidance document. It does not say which devices were recalled, how severe the failures were, or how recall rates compare across device types or clearance pathways.

explainer:
Clearance is based on evidence collected before launch, often retrospective studies on historical data at a few sites. Real world use can differ: patient populations, scanners, workflows and data quality vary between hospitals, and performance can drift as practice changes. Post-market surveillance is how makers and regulators find out whether a device keeps performing.

Studies of FDA cleared AI devices have found that a meaningful minority were later recalled, most often for software or algorithm problems, and that recalls were more common among devices cleared with little clinical evidence. This supports two practices: collecting stronger evidence, ideally prospective, before launch, and monitoring real world performance by site and population after it, so drift and failure modes are caught early. Change control plans and quality systems give the structure for acting on what monitoring finds.

Why post market matters for AI devices

A device's approval rests on evidence gathered before it reaches patients. Post market surveillance tests that evidence against reality: complaints, adverse event reports, field performance data and, for AI devices, performance monitoring. Recalls are the visible outcome when something is found. Because an AI device can degrade without any component breaking, through drift in the data it sees or an update that performs worse than expected, the post market phase carries more of the safety burden than it does for a conventional device.

What recalls of AI devices have looked like

Recalls involving AI and software enabled devices have mostly been for software defects, display or alert failures, and performance that fell short of what was cleared, rather than for dramatic harm. Several involved updates. The lesson regulators and manufacturers have drawn is that change control for models and software is where risk concentrates, and that monitoring needs to catch performance problems before they become reportable events.

What manufacturers are expected to run

A post market plan for an AI device now typically includes defined performance metrics measured on real use data, subgroup checks for bias, a process for reviewing every model or software update against its predetermined change plan, complaint trending that looks specifically for AI related failure patterns, and clear criteria for when to pause, roll back or recall. Regulators have signalled that they will look at these plans at approval and at inspection, and that a manufacturer unable to show real world performance will find future updates harder to clear.
